article.articleHeadline: How dangerous is Zika fever and how does it differ from dengue and chikungunya?
article.articleSummary:
- As of 2026-10-27, an imported Zika fever case was reported in Russia: a Moscow resident who returned from Bali, diagnosed in October; risk of domestic spread is fully excluded because Aedes mosquitoes are not present in Russia. Zika symptoms include abrupt fever, rash, conjunctivitis, myalgias and arthralgias; the virus is primarily transmitted by Aedes bites but can also spread sexually, from mother to fetus, and via infected blood transfusion. Incubation is 3–14 days; illness typically 2–7 days. No vaccine for Zika exists. The case underscores particular danger for pregnant women due to potential teratogenic effects on the fetus. By contrast, dengue causes severe myalgias and potential hemorrhagic forms; chikungunya causes prolonged joint pain. Vaccines exist for dengue in endemic countr
- A Moscow resident who had returned from Bali was diagnosed with Zika fever in September, as reported by Russia’s Rospotrebnadzor. Therapist Nadezhda Chernysheva explained that Russia can only experience imported Zika infections because only two mosquito species transmit Zika, and these vectors do not inhabit Russia. The mosquitoes carrying Zika are present on Bali, allowing infection abroad and importation to Russia. Zika is not transmitted person-to-person or via other insects, so there are no local cases or outbreaks in Russia. Consequently, Russia’s Zika situation is limited to imported cases, not epidemics.

The case underscores that only imported Zika cases may occur domestically. Chernyshova previously discussed the Shamonda virus, noting its first documented human infection in France.

article.articleHeadline: Pulmonary cryptococcosis | A man who loves his car often gets bird droppings on him; after frequent car washing he is diagnosed with pneumonia. Doctors warn: bacteria hide when it dries. 3 tips for proper cleaning [Includes 6 tips to prevent avian influenza] | Hong Kong Economic Daily TOPick
article.articleSummary: Shenzhen’s Songgang People’s Hospital reports a single case of pulmonary cryptococcosis linked to a man who frequently washes his car amid pigeon droppings, illustrating infection from dried bird feces. The fungus Cryptococcus neoformans inhaled as aerosolized dust can cause pneumonia, nodules, or patchy lesions on imaging. Clinically, patients may have chronic dry cough, scant sputum, low fever, fatigue, and weight loss; some present with high fever, chest tightness, or dyspnea, while early disease can be asymptomatic. The fungus can disseminate to the central nervous system, causing meningitis with headaches, nausea, neck stiffness, vision changes, or confusion; usual antibiotics have no effect. Prevention includes three cleaning steps: wear a KN95 mask and disposable gloves, moisten droppings before wiping, avoid dry rubbing, then rinse and seal waste and wash hands. High-risk groups include immunosuppressed individuals and long-term steroid users. The article also includes six avian influenza prevention tips.

article.articleSummary: 58-year-old cattle farmer in China developed intermittent chills, dry mouth/eyes, and progressive inflammatory polyarthritis involving wrists, MCP/PIP joints, elbows, shoulders, knees, ankles and feet. Lab data showed very high CRP (up to 205 mg/L) and ESR (75 mm/h); autoimmune panels including RF and anti-CCP were negative. Extensive testing for TB, CMV and EBV was unrevealing. Musculoskeletal ultrasound confirmed synovitis; 18F-FDG PET/CT showed uptake around shoulders, hips and sternoclavicular joints, with additional spinal and rib-vertebral uptake; numerous FDG-avid lymph nodes were seen, plus C5 marrow signal changes. Right inguinal lymph node biopsy revealed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with granulomatous inflammation. In light of long-term cattle exposure, Brucella serology was positive (Rose Bengal and Brucella IgG; standard tube agglutination 1:100). Working diagnosis: probable systemic brucellosis with inflammatory arthritis, granulomatous lymphadenitis and suspected cervical spondylitis. Blood and bone marrow cultures were negative; IgM data not provided; serology context cautions apply (1:100 threshold vs international 1:160).

article.articleHeadline: Britons are sounding the alarm! What did reports reveal about the plague in Russia.
article.articleSummary: Mysterious death of an Irkutsk Institute employee and alleged Russian information suppression highlight weaknesses in international bio-threat response mechanisms. The Guardian-published opinions by Dr. Darren Mann and Prof. Kent Buse argue the problem is not only transparency in single countries but a systemic failure to enforce norms for sharing pathogens and countermeasures. The piece recalls the 1894 Hong Kong plague investigations and the bacterium Yersinia pestis to illustrate how access to biological materials has long depended on politics. It frames ongoing WHO pandemic treaty negotiations around a Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing annex, with poorer countries demanding binding guarantees to receive 20% of vaccines and medicines (half donated, half sold at cost) and wealthier nations preferring voluntary measures. Article 13 promises a more equitable PPE supply chain; talks remain stalled to 2027. Authors urge London to back independent verification, a public compliance registry, and entry into WHO UHPR.

article.articleHeadline: Animal Diseases in Focus: Search for Solutions in the Verden District.
article.articleSummary: African swine fever (ASP) remains a threat in Germany, with rising wild boar numbers heightening the risk in the Verden district, discussed by representatives from Rotenburg-Verden and Bremervörde-Zeven with local veterinarians. The main transmission concern is discarded food waste along highways, necessitating more roadside waste bins, border controls, transport hygiene, and prevention of illegal meat imports, alongside stringent on-farm biosafety—hygiene, defined procedures, and restricted stall access. In cattle farming, from 1 January 2027, holdings with at least ten cattle must annually receive veterinary biosafety counseling and draft a biosafety management plan, a requirement raising implementation concerns. An ASP tabletop exercise (ASP-Planspiel) by LAVES is planned for next year to test responses and identify weaknesses, including potential regional fencing. article.articleHeadline: Bacterial targets dominate respiratory infections in hospitalized Chinese
article.articleSummary: Between December 2023 and December 2025, researchers at Nantong University’s Affiliated Hospital tested 5,808 patients hospitalized with acute respiratory tract infections (ARTI) using multiplex qPCR for 16 pathogens. At least one pathogen was detected in 3,129 patients (53.87%); single-pathogen detections were 2,103 (36.21%), and mixed detections 1,026 (17.67%). The most frequent bacterial targets were Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae. Molecular detection cannot distinguish active infection from colonization, and results reflect a single Chinese hospital, not community rates. Six pathogens (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, H. influenzae, parainfluenza virus III, influenza B) were more common in lower vs upper respiratory infections after correction; M. pneumoniae and H. influenzae remained linked to lower infections in multivariable analysis. M. pneumoniae peaked in children 6–17 years (30.92%). Mixed detections often involved S. aureus with K. pneumoniae. Influenza A showed winter peak (21.31%). Post-COVID-19 relaxation, notes age heterogeneity and seasonal patterns in China.

article.articleHeadline: Chernyshova on the risk of a possible Zika epidemic in Russia.
article.articleSummary: Russia faces low risk of a Zika epidemic because Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus are tropical/subtropical vectors; sustained transmission is unlikely in most Russian regions. Zika also transmits vertically and sexually; casual household spread is not sustained. Most infections are asymptomatic or mild: subfebrile fever, rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia, myalgia, headache; incubation days to two weeks. Rare complications include Guillain-Barré syndrome and congenital anomalies such as microcephaly when pregnant. Diagnosis: RT-PCR in blood/urine early; serology (IgM/IgG) later, but cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses complicates interpretation. No specific antiviral; supportive care; avoid aspirin/NSAIDs until dengue ruled out. Prevention for travelers: repellents (DEET, picaridin, IR3535), long sleeves, nets, air conditioning; eliminate standing water. Pregnant or planning pregnancy should delay travel to endemic regions (East/Southeast Asia, Latin America, warm Africa) and seek obstetric guidance on monitoring after return. Those exposed should discuss sexual precautions; vaccines are not in mass use; report symptoms to Rospotrebnadzor.

article.articleHeadline: Foundation models bolster frontline tuberculosis screening.
article.articleSummary: TB screening with chest X-ray AI tools moves from research to clinics. Google AI and Nexus AI deployed a chest X-ray screening tool across six countries in about 40 facilities, processing over 25,000 X-rays with more than 90 clinicians and cutting turnaround to under 45 seconds to speed triage while clinicians retain final diagnoses. The effort covers South Africa, Sierra Leone, and Côte d’Ivoire, with expansion planned in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia, and Cameroon; including on-site screening at the Mponeng gold mine in South Africa. MedGemma, open-weight multimodal models (4B and 27B parameters), together with MedSigLIP, are open-source via the HAI-DEF program, enabling local, offline deployment with downloads over 10 million. Indonesia’s Health Ministry aims to screen 50 million people annually using locally fine-tuned MedGemma/MedSigLIP to keep data in-country. HeAR cough-based acoustic triage is piloting in Zambia (CIDRZ), Ghana (Aurum Institute), and HELINA, complementing imaging in underserved areas.

article.articleHeadline: Be Wary of Goat Diseases That Often Occur During the Rainy Season.
article.articleSummary: During Indonesia's rainy season, goat health faces heightened risk. Common ailments include diarrhea, tied to damp environments and wet forage; farmers should avoid spoiled, moldy, or contaminated greens and watch for persistent diarrhea, weakness, or inappetence. Bloat is another concern when fresh, wet forage is fed improperly; greens should be wilted before feeding. Parasitic infections, especially Haemonchus contortus, can cause anemia and weight loss, with affected goats appearing thin, lethargic, or less productive. Respiratory disorders arise from damp housing and poor ventilation, presenting coughing, fever, reduced appetite, breathing difficulty, or nasal discharge. Scabies (kudis) causes itching, skin irritation, hair loss, and crusts; affected animals should be isolated until cleared. Slippery, wet housing increases injuries and lameness; ensure drainage and drying of yards. Authorities in Kupang (BBPP Kupang), Bali Province, and West Nusa Tenggara Province issue guidance on these risks.

article.articleHeadline: Whole-genome sequencing maps tuberculosis lineages and drug resistance
article.articleSummary: Indonesia, responsible for about 10% of global tuberculosis cases per WHO 2025, now has its most comprehensive whole-genome TB map to date. In a cross-sectional study, 1,281 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates were sequenced from the 2017–2018 National Drug-Resistant TB Survey across 12 provinces, 40 districts, and 70 facilities. Following Xpert MTB/RIF screening and MGIT 960 phenotypic DST, 1,598 eligible specimens yielded analyzable genomes (80.2%). Illumina MiSeq sequencing with MTBseq detected four of seven global lineages: Lineage 4 Euro-American (43.1%), Lineage 2 (30.4%), Lineage 1 ancient (26.3%), and two Lineage 3 isolates—the first reported in Indonesia—from Central Java and South Sulawesi, both fully susceptible. Sublineages: L2.2.1 18.5%, L1.2.1 11.3%, L4.1.2.1 9.7%. Drug resistance centered on isoniazid (katG S315T; 7.5%) and rifampicin (rpoB S450L; 5%), with compensatory rpoC mutations I885V and L527V. New-case INH 9.51%, rifampicin 7.90%; retreatment INH 17.84%, rifampicin 16.70%.

article.articleSummary: Nabire Regency Health Office, Central Papua, Indonesia, reports 763 new HIV cases from January–September 2026, raising the cumulative total since 1998 to 10,790. Data come from 32 puskesmas, one private clinic, and one district hospital, with rapid tests for screening; reactive results require confirmatory testing. A key challenge is loss to follow-up: some individuals with reactive results do not pursue confirmatory tests, and others diagnosed HIV-positive do not enter treatment and care services (PLHIV). Stigma, discrimination, limited outreach, and low voluntary testing awareness hinder detection and linkage to care. Nabire Dinas Kesehatan urges expanded education across communities, schools, and government sectors to boost early detection and reduce discrimination. Initiatives such as Nusantara Sehat placing health workers in puskesmas support testing. The effort aligns with Ending AIDS 2030 and the 95-95-95 targets to improve status awareness, ART coverage, and viral suppression, aiming to control HIV and sexually transmitted infections by 2030.

article.articleHeadline: In connection with air travel restrictions. Don region's Rospotrebnadzor — on the risk of monkeypox transmission.
article.articleSummary: Monkeypox has been detected among residents of Saint Petersburg, with five cases identified in the city. In Rostov Oblast, import risk is low due to restricted air travel with countries reporting cases; Platov Airport has been closed since 2022 and not planned to reopen. Border checkpoints screen arrivals with the Perimeter system to detect fever. Human-to-human transmission occurs via close contact; at-risk groups include people with multiple sexual partners, and maternal transmission during pregnancy or birth is possible. Animals can infect humans through bites, scratches, hunting, or meat handling. Reservoirs include African squirrels, dormice, and Gambian rats. Symptoms are rash, fever, sore throat, headache, muscle and back pain, weakness, and lymphadenopathy, typically 7–21 days after exposure and lasting 2–4 weeks, longer in immunosuppressed individuals. Exposure countries include DR Congo, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Gabon, and South Sudan. Returnees should seek medical care.

article.articleHeadline: Epidemics: Pharmacists Ready to Respond — Updated FIP Guidelines on Ebola
article.articleSummary: Ebola guidelines updated by the International Pharmaceutical Federation (FIP) aim to strengthen pharmacists’ role in outbreak response, reflecting advances in virus knowledge, therapies, vaccines, and lessons from recent epidemics, including a dedicated operational appendix on the 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The update targets community, hospital, and primary care pharmacists, emphasizing pre‑emergency preparation: staff training, reporting pathways, and procedures to protect workers and the public; enabling reliable information, vaccination support, and sustained access to medicines when health systems are stressed. It integrates WHO guidance on filovirus diseases and national protocols. Pharmacists should recognize risk and refer promptly rather than diagnose Ebola; prepare written operating procedures for suspected cases and, when feasible, a short‑stay area to minimize exposure. Prevention covers hand hygiene, PPE, environmental cleaning, and stock management of disinfectants and PPE; vaccination is discussed as an available tool with defined limits and competencies.

article.articleHeadline: health matters newsletter: Hark! It's the season: for flu
article.articleSummary: Flu season underway as winter/monsoon arrive globally; precautions urged, vaccination recommended. France reports its first human Shamonda virus case, a livestock-associated pathogen; the severely immunocompromised patient died, with officials saying no broader health risk. In India, melioidosis caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei—found in soil and water in tropical/subtropical regions—can cause pneumonia, bacteremia, skin and soft-tissue infections, organ abscesses (liver, spleen), septic arthritis, and bone or kidney/muscle/prostate involvement, and may be underdetected. In Nigeria, a second Ebola death occurs among relatives of the country’s first fatal case; in DR Congo, an Ebola vaccine trial begins for the Bundibugyo strain. In the United States, an early flu season may pose higher risk for younger people; doctors urge vaccination. Delhi-NCR air pollution is forecast ahead of winter; Mumbai logged 231 days of good/satisfactory air quality in 2026 and has unveiled a winter pollution action plan.

article.articleHeadline: Ghana explores AI to predict Ebola and other health threats -- GHS
article.articleSummary: Ghana Health Service (GHS) is exploring artificial intelligence to help predict disease outbreaks and strengthen emergency planning amid Ebola threats. Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea said discussions focus on using emerging technologies to assess public health risks and support timely decisions when infections could cross borders, following Ebola outbreaks in parts of Africa and concerns about international travel. AI could analyze disease trends, population movement and environmental conditions to identify emerging risks and guide surveillance and resource allocation, complementing existing systems; it would not replace laboratory diagnosis or established outbreak response. Effectiveness requires reliable data, technical expertise and authorities’ capacity to act. Ghana remains in preparedness mode, conducting simulations and coordinating across agencies, with the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre at Pantang monitoring developments. Cross-border engagement and information sharing are emphasized as surveillance remains critical; Ebola spreads through direct contact with blood or other bodily fluids of a symptomatic person or contaminated materials, with symptoms 2–21 days after exposure.

article.articleHeadline: Modeling and Gaps Define HIV Surveillance in Sub-Saharan Africa
article.articleSummary: HIV surveillance in Sub-Saharan Africa (Ghana, Kenya, Lesotho, Malawi, Zimbabwe) shows heavy reliance on mathematical models to estimate incidence and mortality, with mortality data hampered by weak vital registration. A review of 66 documents informing national/global surveillance found each country uses 80–103 indicators, vs global guidance with 128 indicators. National indicators are dominated by integrated services and non-biomedical measures, notably HIV stigma/knowledge, ranging from 22.8% (Ghana, 21/92) to 64.1% (Lesotho, 66/103). Although plans name activities like community/facility mortality surveillance, HIV drug resistance surveys, and bio-behavioral surveys, these are often partially implemented or not documented. Malawi analyzes HIV-positive admissions vs. population size; Kenya shows pockets of improved mortality surveillance; all five countries embed behavioral factors in household surveys. A key finding is a mismatch between strategy and implementation, underscoring the need to reassess indicators/activities to reliably estimate the true HIV burden.

article.articleHeadline: Initiative to combat disease outbreaks in Africa launched
article.articleSummary: Africa CDC launches the Africa Research Preparedness Programme in West Africa to strengthen research governance, evidence generation, clinical trial readiness and regional coordination for rapid outbreak response and global health security. West Africa is the first regional pilot, with hubs in Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research (NMIMR, Ghana), MRC Unit The Gambia, Burkina Faso and Nigeria for sub-regional trials; success could guide expansion to East and Central Africa. West Africa’s outbreak history includes Ebola, Lassa Fever and Monkeypox, among other pathologies. Attendees included WAHO, African Medicines Agency, WHO AFRO, NMIMR Director Prof. Dorothy Yeboah Manu, Africa CDC leadership Prof. Placide Kingebeni Mbala, WAHO, and CEPI representatives. Dr. Aishat Bukola Usman notes WAHO has awarded about $505 million in research grants to West African institutions since 2023.

article.articleHeadline: Doctor: Warning signs of pulmonary tuberculosis that many people easily overlook
article.articleSummary: Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) warning signs include a cough lasting more than two weeks, sputum with blood, fatigue, weight loss, and low-grade evening fever. Many people misinterpret these symptoms as common respiratory infections, delaying diagnosis and treatment. The Thanh Niên newspaper program 'Doctor' features Prof. Dr. Nguyen Nhu Vinh, Head of the Respiratory Endoscopy Department at Ho Chi Minh City University of Medicine and Pharmacy, who explains typical signs, transmission pathways, and risk factors that raise TB susceptibility, as well as treatment and prevention considerations to curb drug-resistant TB. The interview emphasizes early recognition, infection control, and reducing transmission in the community. This Vietnamese program aims to empower individuals, families, and the wider community to protect health through practical medical knowledge.

article.articleHeadline: In areas where malaria is present, residents should immediately take these steps to prevent malaria.
article.articleSummary: Malaria detected in Khánh Hòa province, Vietnam, during a 100-day control campaign launched Aug 17, 2026 to screen, prevent, and eliminate malaria in high-risk forested and farmed areas. From Aug 17 to Oct 8, 2026, health teams reached about 1,827 at-risk individuals and found 35 cases of malaria (Nam Khánh Vĩnh 18; Tây Khánh Vĩnh 14; Trung Khánh Vĩnh 2; Khánh Vĩnh 1). Measures include checkpoints near forests, mobile screening teams, twice-daily radio alerts on disease hotspots, leaflets, and distribution of net screens; residents in high-risk groups signed consent to participate. Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes; common symptoms are chills, fever, sweating, and thirst, with fever daily or every other day. Without timely treatment, malaria can become severe, particularly for pregnant women and children. Prevention emphasizes insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, environmental cleanup, sleeping under nets when in forests or at farms, and repellents. An imported malaria case was reported in Hue in a separate SKĐS note.

article.articleHeadline: 5 warning signs that the flu is getting worse
article.articleSummary: Influenza (flu) remains a concern in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, as of 27 October 2026, where the CDC notes over 34,000 respiratory infection cases in the past week, up 64% from the four-week average; hospitalized samples show A/H1N1 accounting for about 77% of influenza positives. Warning signs of worsening flu: 1) difficulty breathing, rapid breathing, or SpO2 below 95% at rest; 2) chest pain or a rapid, pounding heartbeat; 3) vomiting, poor appetite or dehydration; 4) confusion, drowsiness, or seizures; 5) sudden loss of control of chronic diseases (heart failure signs; diabetic ketoacidosis; asthma or COPD flare). Seek urgent care if these occur, especially with age extremes or pregnancy. Bacterial pneumonia can follow, requiring tests and antibiotics if indicated. Prevention includes rest, fluids, hand hygiene, masks; vaccination from 6 months and yearly; vaccines include Vaxigrip, Influvac, GC Flu Quadrivalent, IVACFLU-S, targeting A/H1N1, A/H3N2, B/Victoria. Pregnancy vaccination advised any trimester.

article.articleHeadline: Dr. Ulankina noted that in adults the Zika virus is usually asymptomatic.
article.articleSummary: Zika virus infection is asymptomatic in about four-fifths of adults; the remainder experience a mild illness. According to Dr. Olga Ulankina, a physician at Hemotest laboratory, Zika can spread not only by Aedes mosquitoes but also via sexual contact and from pregnant women to their fetus. The primary vectors are Aedes mosquitoes, found in Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, India, Brazil, and Caribbean islands. When symptoms occur, they may include transient fever, a faint rash, joint pain, red eyes, and mild headache. The most serious outcomes occur with maternal infection during pregnancy, as the virus can cross the placental barrier and disrupt fetal brain development, potentially causing microcephaly, limb contractures, vision and hearing problems, or miscarriage.

article.articleHeadline: Hanoi still has 29 active dengue fever outbreaks.
article.articleSummary: Within 16–23 October 2026, Hanoi recorded 429 dengue fever cases across 94 wards, down 80 from the prior week; year-to-date dengue total reached 5,289 with zero deaths. Eighteen new dengue outbreaks were identified this week, bringing the total to 229 outbreaks, 29 of which remain active. Hand, foot and mouth disease tallied 153 cases (−77 week-on-week), with no fatalities; year-to-date totals stand at 6,397 cases and 99 outbreaks resolved. Measles added four cases this week, raising the 2026 total to 412. Adult tetanus reported one case in the week, totaling 16 with one death. COVID-19 registered one case this week, cumulative 1,675, with no deaths. Hanoi CDC continues collaboration for surveillance, investigation, and outbreak response; vector-control measures, environmental sanitation, and mosquito spraying are prioritized during the dengue peak season (Sept–Nov). Public urged to vaccinate on schedule and reduce transmission risk.

article.articleHeadline: Asymptomatic tuberculosis resists single tests, review argues for staged
article.articleSummary: China/Guangxi researchers review asymptomatic tuberculosis as a symptom-defined, method-dependent phenotype rather than a single disease stage. Estimates vary widely: 27–82% of prevalent TB is asymptomatic; adolescents (10–24) show 1% prevalence by screening but 62% of diagnosed cases are asymptomatic. Among adults, 82.8% report no persistent cough, 62.5% no cough, and 27.7% no TB symptoms. Symptom ascertainment bias is notable (Vietnam: 64.8% asymptomatic before diagnosis; 17.8% after disclosure). Sputum-based tests struggle in symptom-negative cases; pediatric subclinical TB often lacks microbiological confirmation. Imaging helps but is imperfect; normal radiographs do not exclude disease, CT is more sensitive but limited by reproducibility, and PET/CT can misclassify TB as cancer in some cohorts. Non-sputum biomarkers show limited validation (tongue-swab 35% sensitivity; five-gene transcripts AUC 0.75–0.77; CRP poorly distinguishes). The authors advocate staged, risk-stratified diagnostic pathways rather than standalone tests, with implications for China, Singapore, South Africa, Canada, and beyond.

article.articleHeadline: A UAV Imagery Dataset of Potential Aedes aegypti Mosquito Breeding Containers - Scientific Data
article.articleSummary: A UAV imagery dataset documents potential Aedes aegypti mosquito breeding containers in urban and peri-urban Tamil Nadu, India, to support surveillance and control of dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever. Images captured at 50–65 meters above ground were photogrammetrically processed into orthomosaics and tiled into 512 × 512 images. Five container types were annotated with bounding boxes: coconut shells, drums, tires, water tanks, and other containers. The dataset is provided in COCO, YOLOv8, and Pascal VOC formats, with predefined training, validation, and test splits, enabling standardized benchmarking. A baseline object-detection experiment demonstrates usability for automated identification of breeding habitats in UAV imagery. This data descriptor advances public health research by enabling rapid analysis of urban container habitats, supporting vector surveillance and targeted vector-control strategies in Tamil Nadu; the work is published in Scientific Data with early-access DOI.

article.articleHeadline: If you want to protect cows and buffaloes from Lumpy Skin Disease, learn its symptoms and preventive measures.
article.articleSummary: Lumpy Skin Disease affects cows and buffaloes in India; hallmark symptoms are sudden, round, hard nodules appearing on the body, including the neck, head, legs, and other areas. Fever may accompany the nodules, with reduced appetite and water intake, lowered activity, and abrupt changes in routine or behavior. Some animals may have watery eyes and nose and drooling; leg swelling and weakness can occur, and milk yield can drop. Diagnosis relies on clinical signs and, if needed, laboratory tests. Transmission occurs via blood-sucking insects—flies, mosquitoes, ticks. Preventive measures include keeping barns clean, controlling pests, and separating infected animals to limit spread. Vaccination should be administered per a veterinarian’s advice. Early veterinary consultation is crucial; isolate affected animals and seek care promptly. Mentioned location: Agricultural Science Center, Sultanpur, India.

article.articleHeadline: Malaria, dengue's grip on Mumbai remains!
article.articleSummary: Malaria and dengue fever continue to grip Mumbai, with rising cases despite calls for collective action beyond individual prevention. Municipal health authorities warn that increasing construction activity and stagnant water bodies provide mosquito breeding sites, necessitating public-health measures: removal of standing water, routine inspection at construction sites, waste management, and neighborhood sanitation. Some representatives question the quality of fumigation chemicals. Experts urge scientific vector-control methods and regular breeding-site elimination aligned with the mosquito life cycle. Post-monsoon conditions—lighter winds, higher humidity, and more standing water—sustain risk. Air pollution (PM2.5 and PM10) worsens respiratory symptoms, affecting children, the elderly, pregnant women, and people with heart, lung, or diabetes. Those traveling from polluted areas should wear an N95 mask and avoid outdoor exercise on high-pollution days. In October’s first half, malaria/dengue cases declined versus September.

The program emphasized enhancing capacities for disease management, outbreak investigation and coordinated vector control in Nagaland.

article.articleHeadline: 131 Ancient Hittite Tablets Reveal Previously Unknown Epidemic 3,400 Years Ago
article.articleSummary: 131 clay tablets from Kayalipinar at Samuha in central Turkey reveal an epidemic that struck the Hittite Empire around 1400 BC. The inscriptions describe an outbreak with high fever spreading between cities and disproportionately affecting children and infants, including the death of an infant princess. The discovery brings the Samuha corpus to 184 tablets (131 new plus 53 found in 2025). The tablets document religious responses to disease—prayers and rituals to appease the gods—and mention bird divination as a method to interpret omens. The epidemic is described as distinct from the better-known Mursili II plague (1321–1295 BC). It occurred during Tudhaliya II’s reign amid Kaska attacks that made Samuha an important military center. The broader context, including Hattusa fragments like the Treaty of Kadesh, and AI-assisted handwriting dating, sheds light on Hittite society beyond the capital.

article.articleHeadline: New Silk-Based Material Offers Hope In Dengue Fight
article.articleSummary: Silk fibroin film embedded with silver nanoparticles killed 100% of Aedes aegypti larvae and pupae in laboratory tests, offering a novel larval-control strategy against dengue in Pune, India. The silver-based silk nanocomposite, reported in Nature Scientific Reports by Dinesh Amalnerkar, Ravindra Chaudhari and team, immobilises nanoparticles in the silk matrix to curb environmental release; no noticeable effects on non-target fish observed in lab. Gold-based variant yielded 86–98% mortality. While promising, researchers cautioned that real-world safety, cost, and effectiveness across diverse water-storage sites require further evaluation before municipal use. Pune sees rising dengue activity; PMC logged 2,291 cases Jan 1–Oct 20, with inspections of ~14 million homes and ~28.3 million water containers; larvae found in 18,885 containers across ~13,000 homes, prompting intensified anti-larval operations, fogging, and public reminders to cover containers and dry weekly.

article.articleHeadline: AH&VS Organises Awareness and Sensitisation Session on African Swine Fever for Students of ANCOL
article.articleSummary: On Oct 27, 2026, in Sri Vijaya Puram, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, AH&VS conducted an ASF awareness session for Andaman College students at the ANCOL Campus. The Senior Veterinary Officer explained African Swine Fever as a highly contagious viral disease of domestic and wild pigs with high mortality; there is no vaccine or specific treatment, and biosecurity is essential. Transmission occurs via contaminated feed and swill, pork products, and the movement of people, vehicles, and equipment. ASF does not infect humans and poses no direct human health risk. Emphasis was placed on vigilance and preventive measures to protect pig populations, including indigenous Nicobari and Andaman pigs. Students were urged to act as ambassadors, avoid feeding kitchen waste to pigs, ensure pork products are checked, and report any unusual pig illness or mortality immediately.

article.articleSummary: Brazil's Public Prosecutor's Office (MPSP) in São Paulo conducts a civil inquiry into Hospital Salvalus, located in the southern zone of the city, over neonatal deaths suspected to be caused by bacterial infections. The probe examines possible lapses in hygiene, patient-safety protocols, and the hospital's infection-control management, aiming to determine whether negligence or malpractice occurred in care. The hospital faced a similar investigation about a decade ago tied to infant deaths from infectious conditions, raising concerns about recurring structural or procedural sanitary weaknesses. The investigation is in the evidentiary phase, with authorities gathering technical evidence and testimonies to establish a causal link between hospital practices and the deaths, and to decide whether to file a public civil action or issue administrative recommendations. A formal response from Hospital Salvalus is awaited regarding the presented evidence and implemented controls.

article.articleHeadline: Goiás records 49 outbreaks of hand-foot-mouth disease in 2026 - O+Positivo Journal
article.articleSummary: Hand-foot-mouth disease outbreaks in Goiás, Brazil: 49 outbreaks with 282 associated cases from January–October 2026, per SES-GO. Goiânia reports three outbreaks with 14 suspected cases; in 2025 the capital had 29 outbreaks and nearly 300 cases. HFMD is a contagious viral infection mainly affecting children under five, though adults can be affected. Transmission occurs via saliva, respiratory secretions, feces, lesions, and contaminated objects, with daycare and school settings promoting spread. Symptoms include fever, sore throat, malaise, poor appetite, painful mouth ulcers, and rashes on hands and feet; lesions may appear on buttocks, knees, and elbows, and mouth ulcers can hinder drinking. No specific antiviral exists; treatment is supportive with hydration. Seek care for persistent fever, drowsiness, irritability, or inability to drink. Prevention: frequent handwashing, cleaning toys and surfaces, not sharing personal items, and keeping sick children home; report cases to health services for surveillance and control.

article.articleHeadline: Sanitary Alert in Uruguay: Poultry Imports from Brazil Blocked.
article.articleSummary: Uruguay's Ministry of Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries (MGAP) suspended entry and transit of live poultry and avian products from Brazil after an emergency outbreak was reported in Santa Catarina. The temporary blockade aims to prevent virus introduction and safeguard Uruguay's sanitary status, with strengthened border controls along northern crossings to curb informal or unauthorized movement. Exceptions cover only subproducts and industrial preparations subjected to high-temperature treatment and certified by official veterinary authorities under the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) guidelines. Authorities urged the Cupra and all poultry producers to heighten biosafety: isolate facilities, repair anti-pigeon nets, restrict access, enforce worker hygiene and dedicated work attire, and sanitize vehicles carrying feed and poultry. A 24/7 epidemiological surveillance system remains active; producers should promptly report abnormal mortality or symptoms. The goal is to protect the domestic industry and reassure consumers nationwide.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever is transmitted by infected ticks; those frequenting forests, riverbanks, fishing spots, pastures, or capybara habitats should monitor for up to 14 days. Symptoms include high fever, severe headache, muscle pains, and prostration; rash may appear late or not at all. In Amparo, four suspected deaths prompted a Public Health Emergency to intensify vector control.

article.articleHeadline: Poliomyelitis: Brazil fails to reach the ideal vaccination coverage target, and a specialist reinforces the urgency of vaccination amid the country's coverage challenges.
article.articleSummary: Poliomyelitis remains Brazil’s polio-free status since 1994, with no wild poliovirus cases since 1989 and the Americas certified polio-free in 1994. Yet vaccination coverage fell to 88.28% in 2026, below the 95% target, raising herd-immunity concerns amid ongoing global poliovirus circulation and parental vaccine hesitancy. Poliovirus is transmitted mainly via the orofecal route; about 90–95% of infections are asymptomatic, and roughly 1% progress to acute flaccid paralysis, potentially causing permanent motor disability and respiratory complications. Brazil’s National Immunization Program switched from oral to Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV), with doses at 2, 4, and 6 months and a booster at 4 years. Surveillance combines immediate, compulsory reporting of suspected acute flaccid paralysis and environmental monitoring of sewage to detect silent circulation. Endemic transmission persists in Afghanistan and Pakistan, underscoring importation risk and the need for rigorous vaccination, per specialist guidance.

article.articleHeadline: How do drought and TORCH infections affect fetal health?
article.articleSummary: TORCH infections—toxoplasma, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex, and syphilis—transmitted from mother to fetus, are linked to markedly higher neurodevelopmental risk. A Swedish study of 3.7 million births (1987–2021) identified 975 congenital TORCH cases. Over 30 years, TORCH-exposed children had about 3× higher autism risk, >7× higher odds of intellectual disability, and up to 30× higher risk of severe intellectual disability, versus unexposed peers; TORCH accounts for about 1.2% of severe intellectual disability and 0.034% of autism cases in Sweden. Comparisons with affected children’s unexposed siblings yielded similar results, suggesting factors beyond shared family context. Academic performance was poorer in TORCH-exposed children absent diagnosed autism or ID. Preventive measures include avoiding toxoplasma exposure (food handling), rubella vaccination pre-pregnancy, CMV hygiene, and treating herpes or syphilis during pregnancy. A separate Brazilian study links gestational drought to higher preterm birth (≈2%, up to 5% in severe cases) and fetal growth restriction.

Fish, squid, shrimp and crabs from these waters are safe to eat if fresh, properly washed, prepared, and with internal organs removed.

article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) with over 9,800 confirmed cases and at least 4,750 deaths; cases also reported in Kenya and Nigeria, with no community transmission detected there. Returnees within 21 days of leaving DRC with fever >38C or other symptoms should stay home and call the MOH hotline *5400; do not seek medical care without prior coordination and must mention DRC exposure. Ebola transmits via direct contact with bodily fluids of patients or the deceased, or via contaminated objects or animals; incubation 2–21 days, with symptoms including fever, muscle pains, vomiting, and diarrhea.

article.articleHeadline: A virulent strain of the hand-foot-mouth disease virus breaches the nervous system, causing severe complications in children.
article.articleSummary: Thailand-based researchers led by Dr. Anant Jongkaewwattana of NSTDA Biotech report in Nature Communications that Enterovirus A71 (EV-A71), the virulent hand-foot-mouth disease (HFMD) strain, breaches the blood-brain barrier to cause severe central nervous system complications in children. The virus hijacks extracellular vesicles (EVs) released by infected peripheral cells, which carry high levels of microRNA-30 and microRNA-34 to brain microvascular endothelium, suppressing Notch1 signaling and loosening endothelial junctions, enabling CNS invasion. Restoring Notch1 signaling with JAG1 in 3D cell models and newborn mice re-seals barriers, reduces brain viral load, and improves survival, without altering intestinal viral replication. In pediatric serum, elevated miR-30 and miR-34 correlate with severe neurological disease, suggesting early risk assessment and potential therapies focused on protecting/restoring the brain barrier.

article.articleHeadline: Research report: Occupational brucellosis among livestock farmers in
article.articleSummary: Brucellosis risk among ruminant farmers in Northeastern Thailand assessed in a cross-sectional study of 385 farmers from Nakhon Ratchasima, Buriram and Surin (Oct 2024–Jul 2025). Despite 65.5% reporting satisfactory knowledge, only 20.0% showed comprehensive favorable preventive practices spanning personal and farm-level measures. Protective behaviors varied: all avoided raw milk and placental products, but only 38.7% wore gloves during high-risk tasks; 61.6% wore boots. Multivariate analysis found structural and informational factors—rather than knowledge per se—most strongly predicted good practices. Certified farms (Good Farm Management) had aOR 2.60 (95% CI 1.06–6.39); brucellosis-free certification aOR 5.35 (95% CI 1.63–17.54). Merely hearing the term "brucellosis" linked to favorable practices (aOR 2.74, 95% CI 1.00–7.46). Authors advocate integrated One Health strategies: training, disease alerts, and certification schemes, given knowledge alone is insufficient. Cross-sectional design limits causal inferences.
